proposals.relationship: Le Goff explicitly uses Goody’s Bagre research to explain oral remembering as narrative reconstruction rather than mechanical verbatim repetition.
proposals.evidence_note: Sustained named use in Memória, printed 429–430, alongside 427–428. This credits a specific analytical resource; it does not endorse a universal oral/written divide or establish every claim about LoDagaa culture. Goody’s underlying 1977 article is not independently read.

proposals.relationship: Le Goff draws on Yates’s account of artificial memory and its Renaissance transformations, including her interpretations of memory theatres and Bruno.
proposals.evidence_note: Sustained attributed use and explicit praise, printed 458–460. Yates’s reconstructions remain her interpretations as used by Le Goff; neither their universal acceptance nor her entire hermetic account is asserted. The cited 1966 book is not newly read.

proposals.relationship: Le Goff treats collective memory as both a historical resource and an object of power, calling for historical inquiry that broadens access to social remembering.
proposals.evidence_note: Complete Memória conclusion, printed 475–478. This records his specific program, not sole foundation of memory studies; it preserves the difference between historical inquiry and collective memory.
primary_locators: Portuguese 1990, §6 “Conclusão: o valor da memória,” printed 475–478; PDF zero-based 408–410
